name: Ferns
notes: The archetypal ferns by situation: tree ferns of cloud forest and temperate rainforest, bracken of every dry hillside and burn, the sword and lady ferns of the forest floor, staghorn and bird's nest on tropical trunks, royal fern in bogs, maidenhair on wet rock and cave mouths, mosquito fern on still water. Spore plants: no flowers, spread by wind, need wet ground to breed.

shrub.name: Silver tree fern

growth.juvenile_note: From a flat heart-shaped prothallus come small simple fronds, then a trunkless rosette of stiff, spreading, 2-3-pinnate fronds whose undersides turn chalky silver-white after 3-4 years (young plants are often green beneath). The slow, dark trunk rises only after several years, clad in the stubs of old frond stalks, often with a skirt of dead fronds.
growth.source: Brock et al. 2016 Forest Ecology and Management (NZ tree fern ecology: C. dealbata trunk growth 3.2 cm/yr, 5-11 cm/yr in warmer or plantation sites; to ~10 m, ages to ~250 yr); DOC silver fern fact sheet (silvering at 3-4 yr, drier open forest); University of Auckland NZ plants

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

shrub.name: Soft tree fern

growth.juvenile_note: Spores give a flat green heart-shaped prothallus in weeks; the first fronds are tiny and simple, then increasingly divided. ground.name: Bracken

growth.juvenile_note: Young plants appear 6-7 weeks after spores land on burnt or disturbed bare soil: the first fronds are small, simple and lobed, becoming finely divided and adult-like after about 18 weeks. After up to 10 fronds a rhizome starts, which may grow 2 m in the first year; by year two the patch can be about 2 m across, sending up single, triangular, much-divided fronds from underground.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Pteridium aquilinum (young plants 6-7 weeks after spores shed; adult-like fronds after 18 weeks; rhizome to 217 cm in year 1; spores usually in the 3rd-4th season; cover under 5% below 25% of full sun); Wikipedia (individual rhizomes live up to 72 yr; colonies 650 to over 1,400 yr old).

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

ground.name: Sword fern

growth.juvenile_note: Spores sprout on moist humus or rotting logs into heart-shaped prothalli; the first fronds are tiny and simple to few-lobed, then short, once-pinnate fronds with small, eared, bristle-toothed pinnae. A young plant is a small evergreen rosette of a few stiff, dark green fronds from a short upright rhizome, adding fronds each spring until it becomes the big fountain-shaped clump.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Polystichum munitum (spores first produced at 1-5 yr; fronds 20-250 cm, sometimes 75-100 per plant, evergreen for several years; optimum under 3% light, grows in up to 40% sun); Wikipedia (fronds 50-180 cm, live 1.5-2.5 yr). Clump growth rate and lifespan estimated.

ground.name: Lady fern

growth.juvenile_note: Spores sprout in 10-15 days into heart-shaped prothalli on damp soil; about 3 months later the first tiny fronds unroll, simple and fan-lobed, then pinnate. ground.name: Ostrich fern

growth.juvenile_note: Green, short-lived spores germinate within days into heart-shaped gametophytes; the sporeling's first fronds are tiny and simple, then small pinnate fronds unroll from a little crown. It builds a stout upright crown that each spring unrolls a shuttlecock (vase) of feathery sterile fronds, with stiff brown fertile fronds in the middle from autumn; underground stolons start new crowns nearby.
growth.source: Wikipedia Matteuccia (sterile fronds 100-170 cm, fertile fronds 40-65 cm develop in autumn, persist over winter and shed spores in early spring; lateral stolons form new crowns and dense colonies on riverbanks); fern sporeling timings and ages estimated

ground.name: Royal fern

growth.juvenile_note: Short-lived green spores germinate within 1-3 days into heart-shaped prothalli on wet mud; the first fronds are tiny, fan-shaped and lobed, then once-pinnate. Over several years it builds a tufted crown of tall, bipinnate, pale-green fronds with oblong leaflets; new fronds unroll coppery-red and woolly, and fertile tips carry rust-brown, flower-like spore clusters.
growth.source: SANBI PlantZAfrica (green spores germinate within a day; grows in shade or full sun if wet; 1.5 m, to 3.3 m in Europe); Illinois Wildflowers (spreads slowly, crowns live to ~100 years); years to full size and first fertile fronds estimated from Osmundaceae cultivation

ground.name: Mosquito fern

growth.juvenile_note: A tiny floating sporophyte: a pinhead of overlapping two-lobed scale leaves with hair-fine dangling roots, rising from a sunken megaspore or, far more often, a fragment breaking off an older plant. In days it branches into a 1-2 cm feathery triangle of bluish-green scales that blush red in strong sun and cold, soon locking with others into a velvety floating mat.
growth.source: Wikipedia (plants 1-2 cm, branch and fragment freely, cover lakes within months, die back in winter and survive as submerged buds); Azolla literature (Lumpkin & Plucknett 1980) for doubling times of ~2-5 days and late-summer sporocarps; megaspore-to-sporophyte time estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Spores germinate over 2-7 weeks into heart-shaped prothalli on wet bark and moss; 3-6 months after sowing tiny, simple, spoon- to strap-shaped, apple-green fronds appear. epiphyte.name: Resurrection fern

growth.juvenile_note: Spores sprout on moss and bark of oak limbs into tiny heart-shaped prothalli; the first fronds are small, simple to shallowly lobed and leathery, then once-pinnatifid fronds with grey-scaly undersides. A slender creeping rhizome (about 2 mm thick) branches along the bark into a mat. In drought the fronds curl up grey-brown and look dead, turning green again within a day or two of rain.
growth.source: Wikipedia Pleopeltis polypodioides (fronds to 25 x 5 cm; rhizome 2 mm; survives losing up to 97% of its water and rehydrates in 24-48 h; spores summer to autumn; rhizome pieces root). Spore-to-plant time, growth and lifespan estimated from epiphytic Polypodiaceae.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

epiphyte.note_habit: 1 Oct (Mike's play): an EPIPHYTE — a creeping mat of small leathery fronds on the upper side of big limbs, classically live oak, also cypress, other hardwoods and rock; never ground cover. 'Resurrection': in a dry spell the fronds curl and go grey-brown and can lose most of their water, then green and unfurl within hours of rain. The tropical dry forest copy had it in the ground tier, and as the first file loaded it set the tier for the whole game; all four copies now agree.

desiccation.source: Pleopeltis polypodioides: poikilohydric, desiccation-tolerant; in drought the fronds roll inward and show the grey-brown, densely scaled underside, and can lose up to ~97 % of their water; rehydrated by rain they flatten and turn green within hours, fully within about a day (USDA Forest Service / university extension accounts; Stuart 1968; Muslin & Homann 1992)
desiccation._note: Design 1 Oct §CD (Mike: it behaves as it does in real life). wet_rain_mm_h: local rain (WeatherSim.local_weather) at or above this counts as wetting. Dry: after curl_starts_game_h without rain the fronds begin to roll; by dry_after_game_days they are fully rolled (dry_curl 0-1) and dry_color with the scaly underside showing (dry_underside_shows). Rain: unfurling starts within unfurl_starts_game_h and the plant is flat and green by green_after_game_h. humidity_slows: fog and high humidity stretch the drying. dormant_when_dry: no growth while dry. First guesses on real timings; the designer tunes.

epiphyte.name: Climbing fern

growth.juvenile_note: Heart-shaped green gametophytes on moist soil; the sporeling's first leaves are tiny fan-shaped or two-lobed blades on hair-thin stalks, not climbing at all. Later fronds have a wiry rachis that twines up shrubs like a vine stem, bearing lacy, triangular, finely lobed pinnae; fertile pinnae with fringed, sporangia-bearing margins come higher up. Frost browns the fronds back to the rhizome.
growth.source: USDA FEIS Lygodium spp. review (gametophytes sexually mature within 5 wk of germination, sporophytes produced through week 12; fronds 1-30 m; killed by frost, dead fronds stay draped; fertile June-Sept in the Carolinas); Lott et al. 2003 Am. J. Bot. 90:1144 (reproductive biology); EPPO datasheet

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators

epiphyte.name: Whisk fern

growth.juvenile_note: Spores germinate underground into a tiny (under 2 mm), colourless, branching gametophyte fed by mycorrhizal fungi. The young sporophyte pushes up a few thin, green, rootless stems that fork again and again into leafless 'whisks' with ribbed branches and tiny scale-like bumps, from a brown rhizome in rock cracks, tree-fern trunks or palm leaf bases; yellow, 3-lobed spore cases follow.
growth.source: Wikipedia Psilotum and P. nudum (subterranean mycoheterotrophic gametophyte under 2 mm; sporophyte to 30 cm or more, leafless, with a rootless rhizome; three-lobed synangia with yellow-white spores; epiphytic in the tropics, in rock crevices in temperate areas). Timings and lifespan estimated.
